body.h: Why a checklist beats a spec sheet
body.text: An air fryer listing is written to sell, so it leads with the numbers that sound impressive and buries the numbers that decide the purchase. This checklist is the short list: seven figures, all of them printed on the listing page itself, that tell you whether a machine fits your counter, your household and your evening. Nothing here needs a review unit or a taste test - only a tape measure and two minutes with the listing.

body.h: Number one: capacity - and the unit trap
body.text: Capacity is the headline number and the easiest one to misread, because listings mix units freely. The dual-basket unit in this set is titled as a 6-quart machine made of two independent 3-quart baskets, while its details table shows 6 liters; the single basket lists 8 quarts; the French-door oven lists 24.6 liters in its details while its title names a 26QT oven. Carry the unit along with the number, and compare like with like before you compare anything else.

body.h: Number two: counter depth
body.text: Depth is the number that decides where the machine can physically live. The three products on this site list depths of 13.38, 16.9 and 12.75 inches respectively - a spread of more than four inches between the shallowest and the deepest. Measure the counter you actually have, including the plug and the wall clearance, and read the listed depth as a hard floor.

body.h: Numbers three and four: width and height
body.text: Width and height decide the rest of the fit: whether two machines can sit side by side, and whether the unit slides under a cabinet. The listings show 11.81 by 10.63 inches for the dual basket, 15.8 by 14.8 inches for the French-door oven, and 13.5 by 10 inches for the single basket. Check height against the underside of your cabinets with the machine's own listed figure, not a photo.

body.h: Number five: how the cavity is divided
body.text: How the cooking space is divided shapes how a weeknight actually runs. The dual basket splits into two independent 3-quart baskets; the single basket is one 8-quart space; the French-door oven is one tall cavity with front doors. Two baskets mean a main and a side finishing together; one cavity means a roast or a pizza. Neither is better - the right answer is the shape of the meals you cook most.

body.h: Number six: heat range and stated functions
body.text: The stated heat range tells you what is possible: the dual basket lists 200 to 450 degrees, and the single basket lists 200 to 400 degrees with a 450-degree Hi-Fry option. Function counts are shakier ground - one listing here says 24 cooking functions in its title and 25 cooking pre-sets in its feature section, and this site reports both counts rather than picking one. Count the functions you will actually use; the tally on the box is not the point.

body.h: Number seven: cleanup
body.text: Cleanup is the friction you live with daily, and listings describe it in one clause worth reading twice. The dual basket and the single basket both list nonstick, dishwasher-safe baskets; the oven's title names six included accessories while its own page description says seven, so quote neither count as settled. If the parts that touch food cannot go in your dishwasher, the machine will cost you minutes every evening.

body.h: The feature row is a list of labels, not a specification
body.text: Every air fryer listing has a field labelled Special Feature, and it is a comma-separated list of names the seller selected, not measurements. The three listings this site tracks carry nine distinct names between them. The dual-basket machine lists 2Min Button, Automatic Shut-Off, Dual Zone Features, Hi-Fry and Mute. The French-door oven lists Automatic Shut-Off, Programmable, Temperature Control and Timer. The single-basket machine lists Automatic Shut-Off, LED Shake Reminder and Programmable. No row states a duration, a decibel figure, a temperature or a number of zones - the field records that a thing exists on the machine, and that is the whole of what it promises.

body.h: When a name does come with a number
body.text: Hi-Fry is the exception, and it is worth understanding why. The single-basket listing puts the figure in the title itself: '450°F Hi-Fry Option for Crispier Results'. On that machine the name arrives with the number attached, so you know what Hi-Fry means as a setting: the upper end of a range whose rest is stated elsewhere as 200-400°F. The dual-basket listing names Hi-Fry in its title and its feature row but attaches no figure there; its stated range, 200-450°F, appears in its own descriptive text. Same word, two different amounts of support on the page - which is the practical lesson of this whole list. A feature name is worth as much as the number printed next to it.

body.h: One name appears on all three listings
body.text: Automatic Shut-Off is the only label all three listings claim. Treat that as a category expectation rather than a differentiator: in this price-and-format band the field is where sellers tick the boxes Amazon offers, and a box three out of three sellers tick tells you the feature is table stakes. It does not tell you the three machines behave alike. The cut-off temperature, the timeout and whether the beep can be silenced are not in that row on any of the three pages.

body.h: Names that appear once, and the question to ask about each
body.text: The singletons are where a listing is genuinely different, and each has one obvious follow-up. Mute on the dual basket: which sounds does it silence, and can it be set back? 2Min Button: a two-minute add, or a two-minute reminder? LED Shake Reminder on the single basket: does it light, sound, or both, and at what point in the cycle? Temperature Control and Timer on the oven, next to a Programmable claim: programmable for how many of its presets? None of those answers is on the page this site reads, so this page does not guess them either. They are in the manual, which the listing links to at most indirectly.

body.h: Titles carry more feature names than the details field does
body.text: Sync Finish and Easy View Windows - the two names people search for when comparing dual-basket machines - do not appear in the dual basket's Special Feature row at all. They appear in its title. The same pattern holds on the oven, whose title segment names a preset count and an accessory count that its details field leaves out. When you compare two listings, read the title as a second, less controlled feature list: it is where the seller puts the claims they most want found, and it changes more often than the table does. This site has seen one of its own tracked titles change wording twice, which is why every quoted title here carries the date it was read.

body.h: Where the definition actually lives
body.text: The oven listing links to a brand store page, and that is the shape of the answer: named features are defined by the manufacturer's own material, not by the marketplace row that advertises them. Before you pay for a machine because of a feature name, open the brand's manual or support page for that model and check three things - what triggers the feature, whether it can be turned off, and what number, if any, the maker attaches to it. If the maker states none, the feature is a behaviour, not a specification, and it should not outweigh a measured figure like capacity or depth in your decision.

body.h: How to use this list on a shortlist of two
body.text: Put the two Special Feature rows side by side and cross out every name both machines claim; what survives is the actual difference, and it is usually one or two items rather than six. Then check each survivor for a number on the page, and treat the ones without a number as questions for the manual. Prices and star ratings are deliberately absent from this site, so the comparison is on listed specifications alone - the live price is always one click away on the listing itself.

body.h: The case
body.text: The French-door oven this site tracks states its function count two ways on one page. Its title has read '24 One-Touch Preset Options' on the two most recent dated readings, and on an earlier reading the same position in the title read '24 cooking functions'. Its 'About this item' section heads the feature list '25 COOKING PRE-SETS'. Amazon states the discrepancy nowhere on the page, and this page will not invent a reconciliation: what a shopper can do is notice that the headline number and the list number are different numbers, in different fields, maintained by the same seller.

body.h: Count the named modes yourself
body.text: Under the 25 heading, the listing names eleven modes: Ribs, Defrost, Bake, Toast, Chicken, Pizza, Pastry, Slow Cook, Roast, Reheat and Keep Warm. Eleven named modes, a heading that says 25 and a title that says 24. The number that should matter to you is the one you can verify by counting on the page, because it is the one that corresponds to buttons you will actually press. If a mode you cook by is not in that list of eleven, neither headline count is going to add it.

body.h: The same page does it again with accessories
body.text: The title segment says 'Six Cooking Accessories Included'. The product description on the same page says seven, and names three of them (an air fry basket, a rotisserie spit and a bake pan) with an 'and more'. This site publishes no accessory count for that reason. It is the same class of problem as the preset count, one field apart: a number in a marketing line that the detail on the page does not sustain.

body.h: And a third time with capacity
body.text: Capacity shows the pattern most clearly, because the unit changes as well as the number. That oven is named 26QT in its title and records 24.6 liters in its details table. The dual basket is named 6 Quart and records 6 liters - and six US quarts and six litres are not the same volume, so both figures cannot describe the same unit. Neither is a rounding error you can ignore when a recipe or a pan has to fit: they are two claims from one seller, and the table row is the one that sits in the field Amazon validates.

body.h: Why titles disagree with themselves over time
body.text: There is a fourth reason not to trust a headline number blindly: the headline moves. This site read one wording of this listing's title on 2026-11-14, a different one on 2026-11-17 and the second wording again on 2026-11-19, with the ASIN unchanged throughout. A screenshot or a quote you copy into a shortlist is therefore only as good as its date. Every number this site publishes carries the page it was read from and the day it was read, including on this article's own table below.

body.h: What to write on your list
body.text: Three rules come out of this. Take measurements from the details table, never from the title, and carry the unit with the figure. Take feature counts from the named list you can count, not from either headline. Date anything you copy, because the seller can change the sentence without changing the product. Applied here: 24.6 liters and 16.9 inches deep are the numbers to plan a counter around, eleven named modes are what the preset list supports, and no accessory count is settled. Prices and ratings are not shown on this site at all, so the listing stays the place where those live.
